subject: physics
title: Internal energy and energy transfers
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: Internal energy and energy transfers — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.3.2.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering Internal energy and energy transfers, specification section 4.3.2.
final_note: You worked through Internal energy and energy transfers — 24 specification statements.

concepts.def: The energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up that system. It is a store held by the particles themselves, not something that flows into or out of the system.
The object, or group of objects, being considered. Internal energy belongs to the system as a whole and is the sum of the energies of every particle inside it.
The energy the atoms and molecules of a system have because they are moving. It is one of the two contributions to the internal energy of the system.
The energy stored because of the positions of the atoms and molecules relative to one another. It is the second of the two contributions to the internal energy of a system.

Internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up a system. Both contributions are included, and they are added over every particle, not averaged.
An energy transfer that changes the energy stored within a system by increasing the energy of the particles that make up the system.
Heating a system either raises the temperature of the system or produces a change of state. While a change of state is taking place the temperature does not rise.

concepts.term: What the temperature increase depends on
concepts.def: If the temperature of the system increases, the increase in temperature depends on three things: the mass of the substance heated, the type of material, and the energy input to the system.

The specific heat capacity of a substance is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of the substance by one degree Celsius. A substance with a large specific heat capacity needs a large energy input for each degree of temperature rise.

change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written in symbols as ∆E = m c ∆θ. It is one of the equations provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet, so it does not have to be recalled, but it must be selected correctly and applied.
The energy transferred to or from a system when its temperature changes, measured in joules, J.
The mass of the substance being heated, measured in kilograms, kg. A mass quoted in grams must be converted to kilograms before it is substituted into the equation.
Specific heat capacity, c, is measured in joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, J/kg °C. The unit itself states the definition: joules needed per kilogram, per degree of temperature rise.
The change in temperature of the system, measured in degrees Celsius, °C. It is the difference between the final and starting temperatures, not the final temperature itself.
A change between the solid, liquid and vapour states of a substance. While it happens, the energy supplied changes the internal energy of the substance rather than its temperature.
The energy needed for a substance to change state. When a change of state occurs, the energy supplied changes the energy stored (internal energy) but not the temperature.
The specific latent heat of a substance is the amount of energy required to change the state of one kilogram of the substance with no change in temperature.

energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, written in symbols as E = m L. Like the thermal energy equation, it is provided on the AQA Physics equation sheet rather than recalled, so the skill tested is choosing it and using it correctly.

concepts.term: Energy, E, for a change of state
concepts.def: The energy transferred while the substance changes state, measured in joules, J.

concepts.term: Mass, m, in E = m L
concepts.def: The mass of substance that changes state, measured in kilograms, kg. As in the thermal energy equation, a mass given in grams must first be converted to kilograms.
Specific latent heat, L, is measured in joules per kilogram, J/kg. There is no per degree Celsius in the unit, because no temperature change takes place.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from solid to liquid.
The specific latent heat for the change of state from liquid to vapour.

Graphs of temperature against time for a substance being heated or cooled steadily. Sloping sections show the temperature changing, so ∆E = m c ∆θ applies. Flat sections show a change of state at constant temperature, so E = m L applies; energy is still being transferred throughout a flat section.

concepts.term: Distinguishing specific heat capacity from specific latent heat
concepts.def: Specific heat capacity is the energy for one kilogram to change temperature by one degree Celsius, in J/kg °C, and applies to sloping parts of a heating graph. Specific latent heat is the energy for one kilogram to change state with no change in temperature, in J/kg, and applies to flat parts of a heating graph.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?
options: The total kinetic energy of all the particles moving inside it
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all its particles
The temperature that the particles inside the system have reached
The energy the system gives out when its surroundings are cooler
mcqs.explain: This is the specification definition: internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.

mcqs.q: Which pair of quantities are added together to give the internal energy of a system?
options: The kinetic energy of every particle and the volume of the whole system
The kinetic energy and the potential energy of every particle present
The heat contained in the system and the temperature it has reached
The temperature of the system and the potential energy of its particles
mcqs.explain: Internal energy is the sum of both contributions, taken over all the atoms and molecules in the system.

mcqs.q: A beaker of pure ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater. What happens to the energy supplied while the ice melts?
options: It increases the energy of the particles and warms the ice above 0 °C
It raises the temperature slowly while the ice is turning into water
It increases the energy of the particles and melts the ice at 0 °C
It is stored as temperature in the beaker until all the ice has melted
mcqs.explain: Heating increases the energy of the particles, and here that produces a change of state rather than a temperature rise.

mcqs.q: Heating changes the energy stored within a system. How does it do this?
options: By adding a quantity of heat that the system then contains inside it
By increasing the energy of the particles that make up the system
By increasing only the potential energy of the particles already present
By raising the temperature, since temperature is the energy stored
mcqs.explain: This is the mechanism the specification states: heating increases the energy of the particles, changing the energy stored.

mcqs.q: Beaker A holds 1 kg of a liquid and beaker B holds 2 kg of the same liquid, both starting at 20 °C. Each is given 8400 J. Which statement is correct?
options: Beaker B rises by twice as many degrees as beaker A does
Both beakers rise by the same number of degrees Celsius
Beaker A rises by twice as many degrees as beaker B
Both beakers finish at exactly the same final temperature
mcqs.explain: For a fixed energy input, ∆θ is inversely proportional to mass, so half the mass gives twice the temperature rise.

mcqs.q: Equal masses of copper and of water are each given 5000 J of energy. The temperature of the copper rises much more than that of the water. Why?
options: Copper has the larger specific heat capacity, so it warms up faster
Copper must have been given more energy than the water was given
The temperature increase depends on the type of material as well
Copper is a metal, so heating it always produces a bigger rise
mcqs.explain: With mass and energy input equal, the remaining factor the specification lists is the type of material, and copper has the smaller specific heat capacity.

mcqs.q: Which equation gives the change in thermal energy of a substance whose temperature changes?
options: ∆E = m L ∆θ
∆E = m c ∆θ
∆E = m ∆θ / c
∆E = c ∆θ / m
mcqs.explain: change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change.

mcqs.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
options: J/kg
J/°C
J/kg °C
J kg °C
mcqs.explain: Joules per kilogram per degree Celsius, exactly as the definition states.

mcqs.q: 2.0 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the water?
A 0.50 kg metal block is given 9200 J of energy and its temperature rises by 40 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
0.30 kg of oil at 15 °C is given 12 000 J of energy. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J/kg °C. What is the final temperature of the oil?
mcqs.explain: ∆θ = 12 000 / (0.30 × 2000) = 20 °C, so the final temperature is 15 + 20 = 35 °C.

mcqs.q: A substance has a specific heat capacity of 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?
options: 900 J raises the temperature of the whole substance by 1 °C
900 J changes the state of one kilogram of it without warming
900 J raises the temperature of one kilogram of it by 1 °C
900 J raises the temperature of one kilogram of it up to 1 °C
mcqs.explain: This is the definition: the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram by one degree Celsius.

mcqs.q: Ice at 0 °C is melting while energy is supplied to it steadily. Which statement is correct?
options: Both the internal energy and the temperature of the ice increase
Neither of them changes, since the temperature reading stays fixed
The temperature increases while the internal energy stays constant
The internal energy increases but the temperature stays at 0 °C
mcqs.explain: During a change of state the energy supplied changes the energy stored but not the temperature.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the specific latent heat of a substance?
options: The energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram by one degree
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram by one degree
The energy required to change the state of a whole sample completely
The energy required to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
mcqs.explain: This is the specification definition of specific latent heat.

mcqs.q: A solid at its melting point has a specific latent heat of fusion of 250 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 200 g of it completely?
mcqs.explain: E = m L = 0.200 × 250 000 = 50 000 J, with the mass converted to kilograms.

mcqs.q: 0.25 kg of a liquid at its boiling point is completely turned to vapour by 575 000 J of energy. What is its specific latent heat of vaporisation, in J/kg?
What is the unit of specific latent heat?
options: J/kg
J/kg °C
J
J °C/kg
mcqs.explain: Specific latent heat is measured in joules per kilogram; no temperature change is involved.

mcqs.q: The specific latent heat of fusion is defined for which change of state?
options: From solid to liquid
From liquid to vapour
From vapour to liquid
From solid to vapour
mcqs.explain: The specification defines specific latent heat of fusion as the change of state from solid to liquid.

mcqs.q: Water in a kettle is at 100 °C and is boiling away to steam. Which quantity is needed to calculate the energy transferred while it boils away?
options: The specific latent heat of fusion of the water
The specific heat capacity of the water used
The specific heat capacity of the steam made
The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water
mcqs.explain: Liquid is changing to vapour at constant temperature, so E = m L with the latent heat of vaporisation.

mcqs.q: A solid is heated steadily from below its melting point until it has all boiled away. Its temperature–time graph has two flat sections. What is happening during the first, lower flat section?
options: The substance is boiling, since boiling always begins before melting
No energy is being transferred to the substance during that time
The substance is melting, so the energy raises its internal energy
The substance is warming very slowly because it takes in less
mcqs.explain: A solid heated from below its melting point melts first, and during that change of state the temperature stays constant.

mcqs.q: A hot liquid is left to cool. Its temperature–time graph falls, then stays flat for several minutes, then falls again. What does the flat part show?
options: The liquid has stopped losing energy to its surroundings
The liquid has cooled to the temperature of the room
The liquid is boiling, so its temperature cannot change
The liquid is freezing, and energy is still leaving it
mcqs.explain: A plateau part-way down a cooling curve is a change of state at constant temperature; energy transfer continues throughout.

mcqs.q: How does specific heat capacity differ from specific latent heat?
options: They are the same quantity, simply given two different names
One is measured per kilogram, the other for the whole sample
One applies only to solids, and the other only to liquids
One is for a temperature change, the other for a change of state
mcqs.explain: Specific heat capacity applies while the temperature changes; specific latent heat applies while the state changes at constant temperature.

mcqs.q: 500 g of aluminium is heated and its temperature rises by 20 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the aluminium?
mcqs.explain: ∆E = m c ∆θ = 0.500 × 900 × 20 = 9000 J, once the mass is converted to kilograms.
